title: Common Core SL.CCR.1 Explained
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart unpacks the first Speaking and Listening anchor standard of the Common Core and argues that it is unworkable in a classroom that runs entirely in talk-to-the-teacher mode. His central claim is that productive discussion is not a personality trait but a product of preparation: students who have done the reading, the practice problem, or the quickwrite are the ones ready to contribute. He then reduces the standard to a balance between two conversational moves — expressing your own ideas and building on the ideas of others — and names the two failure modes, the egocentrist who only pushes his own ideas and the 'unremarkable shadow' who only echoes others. The instructional move he proposes is unglamorous and repeatable: teach the two moves explicitly, give students practice in each move separately and together, and give feedback on how they're doing. He closes by noting that his own classroom improvement came from a mix of explicit instruction, frequent debate and discussion, and modelling the balance in how he himself talks with classes. The piece is an early example of his habit of turning a vague standard into two or three teachable behaviors.
points: Stuart's diagnostic claim is that SL.CCR.1 simply cannot be met in a room where students instinctively address the teacher rather than each other — the discussion structure, not the standard, is the blocker.
He reframes preparation as the hidden prerequisite of good discussion: knowledge of the topic, built through homework, quickwrites or notes, is what makes a student ready to speak.

The article's most portable idea is the two-move model — expressing your own ideas versus building on others' — with named failure modes (the egocentrist and the 'unremarkable shadow') that students can recognize in themselves.
His teaching plan is deliberately thin: name the two moves, practice them in isolation and in combination, and give feedback — no new curriculum required.

He credits part of his students' growth to the teacher's own conversational modelling, arguing that much of this standard is taught by how a teacher engages students rather than by instruction about it.
quotes: SL.CCR.1 is impossible to carry out if your class operates only in talk-to-the-teacher mode. (If I were you, I'd probably want to tweet that.)

SL.CCR.1 basically says, “The most productive members of conversations begin by being prepared.” This may mean reading the homework, doing the practice problem, completing the quickwrite, or taking notes on the lecture.
Great speaking requires planning. Being a productive group member means preparing to be one.

A bonafide egocentrist ignores the ideas of others and only expresses his/her own. An unremarkable shadow talks only about the ideas of others and seems to have none of his/her own. An effective conversationalist listens to and builds on the ideas of others and expresses his/her own.

Last school year, I used a lot of in-class debates and discussions, and I was amazed at how students began to get better talking to and with each other. This was part due to explicit instruction, part due to frequent practice, and part due to simply striving to balance these two conversational moves as I spoke with my classes. It's amazing how much of this we teach simply by how we engage with our students.
